The Civil Rights Cases of 1883. Five separate cases were consolidated and decided together that year, challenging the Civil Rights Act of 1875, which had prohibited racial discrimination by private businesses in public accommodations. The Supreme Court, voting 8 to 1, struck down the law. Justice Joseph P. Bradley wrote that the 14th Amendment constrains only state action, not private conduct, and that Congress lacked the power to regulate private discrimination. That single ruling gutted the last major civil rights legislation of Reconstruction and opened the door to Jim Crow statutes that could evade constitutional challenge.

The cases arose from discrimination at hotels, railroads, theaters, and similar private businesses. Bradley's reasoning severed Congress's power to protect freedmen from private violence and discrimination, leaving federal civil rights authority in tatters. The decision effectively repealed the Civil Rights Act of 1875 and handed victory to those seeking to roll back Reconstruction gains. Only Justice John Marshall Harlan dissented, warning the decision would facilitate widespread racial oppression.

For nearly 90 years, the Civil Rights Cases stood as law. It wasn't until 1964 that Heart of Atlanta Motel v. United States found a different constitutional hook—the Commerce Clause—to restore federal civil rights enforcement. The damage, however, had already been done. Between 1883 and the modern civil rights era, Jim Crow laws flourished unchecked.
